statement: In people in alcohol withdrawal in placebo-controlled trials published from 1961 to 1983 (most of them of chlordiazepoxide; those in the Cochrane review all randomized), benzodiazepines compared with placebo reduced withdrawal seizures: in a Cochrane review searched to December 2009, 1 of 149 people given a benzodiazepine against 14 of 175 given placebo had a seizure in three trials (risk ratio 0.16, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.69), about 1 against 8 in 100 in the review's illustration (13 against 80 per 1,000), graded moderate quality by the review (Amato et al., 2010; funded by a Rome health authority and the Italian medicines agency; no conflicts declared). An earlier review found 7.7 fewer seizures per 100 people treated (95% CI 3.5 to 12.0 fewer; five trials) and 4.9 fewer cases of delirium per 100 (0.7 to 9.0 fewer; four trials, 3 of 172 against 11 of 186 people, editors' sums) (Mayo-Smith, 1997; a practice guideline of a US medical society, ASAM, with no funding or conflict statement). The two reviews share three trials, and one trial from 1969 supplies most of the events, so they are not independent confirmation. Against other medicines pooled together (trials up to 2009; anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, clonidine, beta-blockers and others), benzodiazepines showed no clear difference in seizures (risk ratio 0.52, 0.21 to 1.31; 12 trials) or delirium (0.65, 0.21 to 1.98; 8 trials); against anticonvulsants alone the estimates leaned towards the anticonvulsants, also without a clear difference (seizures 1.70, 0.39 to 7.37; delirium 1.90, 0.43 to 8.38), and adverse events tended to be more frequent with benzodiazepines (1.31, 0.99 to 1.72). Phenothiazine antipsychotics given alone did not reduce delirium compared with placebo (risk difference 0.0 per 100, −5.8 to +6.6) and were followed by more seizures (11.4 more per 100, 6.2 to 16.6) and more delirium (6.6 more per 100, 2.4 to 10.8) than benzodiazepines or paraldehyde. In the comparisons with other medicines, deaths occurred in 4 of the 32 trials in the mortality analysis. For people already in withdrawal delirium, a narrative review describes the treatment evidence as nine controlled trials from 1959 to 1978 and later uncontrolled studies (Schuckit, 2014). Most trials did not report how allocation was concealed, events were few, outcome definitions predate DSM-IV, and people with serious liver, heart, lung or kidney disease or other drug dependence were usually left out. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In trials from the 1960s to the 1980s, people going through alcohol withdrawal who were given a benzodiazepine, a calming medicine, had fewer seizures than people given dummy pills: about 1 in 100 against about 8 in 100. They also developed delirium less often, about 2 in 100 against 6 in 100. Other medicines were not clearly better or worse at preventing seizures or delirium, but one kind of antipsychotic given on its own was followed by more seizures and delirium than benzodiazepines. The trials were small and old, and few looked at people who already had the DTs.
population: People in alcohol withdrawal in randomized trials published 1961 to 1983 (placebo comparisons) and up to 2009 (comparisons with other medicines), mostly in hospital wards, detoxification units and veterans' hospitals, mostly men, usually without serious medical illness or other drug dependence
exposure: A benzodiazepine (mostly chlordiazepoxide in the placebo-controlled trials; also diazepam and lorazepam)
comparator: Placebo; other medicines (anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, clonidine, beta-blockers and others, pooled); phenothiazine antipsychotics against placebo and against benzodiazepines or paraldehyde
outcome: Withdrawal seizures and withdrawal delirium during the withdrawal episode; adverse events; deaths
magnitude: Amato et al. 2010 (Cochrane, search to December 2009): against placebo, seizures RR 0.16 (0.04 to 0.69), 3 trials, 324 participants, 1/149 against 14/175, I² 0%, GRADE moderate, illustrative 80 against 13 per 1000 (3 to 55); against other drugs, seizures RR 0.52 (0.21 to 1.31), 12 trials, 1228, 5/442 against 37/786; against anticonvulsants 1.70 (0.39 to 7.37), 7 trials, 523; delirium RR 0.65 (0.21 to 1.98), 8 trials, 893, I² 52%; against anticonvulsants 1.90 (0.43 to 8.38), 5 trials, 342; at least one adverse event RR 1.31 (0.99 to 1.72), 18 trials, 919, GRADE low; deaths in 4 of the 32 trials of the mortality analysis (2 with benzodiazepines, 5 with other drugs, editors' sum). Mayo-Smith 1997: risk difference, benzodiazepine against placebo, delirium −4.9 per 100 (−9.0 to −0.7), 4 trials, 3/172 against 11/186; seizures −7.7 per 100 (−12.0 to −3.5), 5 trials, 1/182 against 17/196 (editors' sums from Table 2); phenothiazine against placebo, delirium 0.0 (−5.8 to +6.6), seizures +4.6 (−2.6 to +11.9); phenothiazine against benzodiazepine or paraldehyde, delirium +6.6 (+2.4 to +10.8), seizures +11.4 (+6.2 to +16.6).

evidence.extracted: Mortality against other drugs was analysed in 32 trials (2088 participants) and not pooled; deaths occurred in 4: Golbert 1967 (0 of 12 against 2 of 37), Kaim 1969 (0 of 103 against 2 of 304), Kaim 1972 (0 of 46 against 1 of 142) and Lenzenhuber 1999, an intensive-care trial (2 of 21 on flunitrazepam against 0 of 21 on GHB). The authors call the mortality rate extremely small and the harms data sparse and fragmented.

evidence.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies (Allocation; Blinding; Incomplete outcome data); Methods › Assessment of reporting biases; Characteristics of included studies
evidence.extracted: Of the 64 included randomized trials (4309 participants by the review's count), sequence generation was adequate in 16 and allocation concealment in 13 (unclear in 47, inadequate in 4); selective reporting was not assessed and publication bias was not investigated. Trials had 16 to 537 participants, many enrolled only men, and people with severe liver, heart, lung or kidney disease, epilepsy or dependence on other drugs were commonly excluded. In the largest trial (Kaim 1969) the seizure outcome appears to be analysed only in those who stayed in the trial (arithmetic on the study card).

evidence.locator: Treatment of Withdrawal Delirium, 1st paragraph (p. 2110, continuing on p. 2111)
evidence.extracted: The author states that few double-blind, controlled, prospective treatment trials exist for withdrawal delirium, offering its low prevalence, high treatment costs and a lack of commercial incentive as possible reasons, and that the best evidence is a 2004 review of nine prospective controlled trials conducted between 1959 and 1978, with later uncontrolled studies found in a PubMed search.

risk_of_bias.note: Allocation concealment was unclear in 2 of the 3 trials in the Cochrane seizure pool (the review's own reason for moderate) and adequate in 13 of 64 trials overall; the 1997 review appraised no trial (sc_mayo_smith_1997: AMSTAR 2 critically low); in the largest trial the seizure outcome appears to be counted only in those who stayed; outcome definitions predate DSM-IV.

inconsistency.note: All placebo-controlled trials point the same way (I² 0% for seizures).

indirectness.note: Worded for people in withdrawal in these trials, with the period and the exclusions stated; the treatment of established delirium is not claimed.

imprecision.note: 15 seizures in the Cochrane pool (1 against 14) and 14 delirium cases in the 1997 pool (3 against 11), with a delirium interval reaching 0.7 fewer per 100; the comparisons with other medicines are imprecise in both directions.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by either review; with few small trials it cannot be judged. Not rated down, recorded as unknown.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high. Rated down for risk of bias (unclear concealment, an unappraised older pool, pre-DSM-IV outcome definitions) and imprecision (few events), giving low; the Cochrane review rated the seizure result moderate, downgrading only for concealment. 'Reduces' is used for the placebo comparison because the evidence is randomized and the intervals exclude no effect; the comparisons with other medicines show no clear difference either way and are not claimed as equivalence. Overlap: three trials (Kaim 1969, Sellers 1983, Naranjo 1983) are in both reviews' seizure pools, with different counts for Naranjo 1983 (0/21 against 1/20 in the Cochrane review, 0/15 against 2/15 in the 1997 review), so the two reviews are counted once. Status replicated: several independent trials point the same way, though no single trial was significant on its own. No regimens or doses are given (the reviews' dosing comparisons are left out).
